medium.titulo: Manual vs Automation Testing: Which Does Your Startup Need?
medium.resumo: Here’s a conversation we hear a lot from founders.
medium.conteudo_html:
Here’s a conversation we hear a lot from founders.

“We launched the new feature on Friday. By Monday, three customers had emailed us about the same bug. Should we hire a tester or buy some automation tool?”

Fair question. And the honest answer is: probably a bit of both, just not at the same time.

[Add a real one-line example from your team here, e.g. a bug a client found before you did. This is the single biggest thing that makes a post feel human.]

Let’s break it down without the jargon.

Manual testing: still underrated

Manual testing is exactly what it sounds like. Someone sits with your app and uses it like a real customer would. They click the wrong buttons, type weird things into forms, and notice when something just feels off.

People sometimes treat it as old-fashioned. We don’t. When your product is changing every week, manual testing is often the smartest choice. Writing automated scripts for a screen you’ll redesign next sprint is a waste of everyone’s time.

It’s also the only way to catch the “technically works, but users hate it” problems. A script can tell you the checkout button works. It can’t tell you nobody can find it.

The catch? It doesn’t scale. Once your app has 30 screens and you release every week, your tester ends up re-checking login and payments by hand, again and again. That’s when releases start getting stuck waiting for QA, and good testers get bored.

Automation testing: great, once you’re ready for it

Automation means writing tests once and letting a tool run them for you, usually every time a developer pushes code. Login, signup, payments, search: the boring flows that must never break are perfect for this.

When it’s set up well, it feels like magic. A developer pushes a change at 6 PM, and ten minutes later they know whether they broke something. No waiting for the tester to come in the next morning.

But here’s what tool vendors don’t always mention. Traditional automation needs people who can write and maintain scripts. And scripts are fragile. Change a button’s label or move it a few pixels, and half your tests go red even though nothing is actually broken. We’ve seen teams spend more time fixing their tests than fixing their product.

[Optional: add a short story from your own team about flaky tests or a script that broke after a UI change.]

The quick comparison

If you just want the short version, here it is. Manual testing is cheap to start, but the cost keeps growing with every release because someone has to repeat the same checks by hand. Automation costs more upfront for tools, setup and scripts, but it gets cheaper over time as the same tests run again and again in minutes. Manual testing shines for user experience, exploratory testing and brand-new features, and it handles UI changes easily because a human just adapts. Automation is best for regression and repetitive flows, but traditional scripts often break when the UI changes, and they can’t judge whether something actually feels right to a user. In short, humans bring judgment and machines bring speed.

So what should your startup actually do?

It really depends on where you are. Roughly, it plays out like this.

Just launched or still building your MVP? Stay manual. Your screens will change too often for scripts to survive. Keep a simple checklist of the five things that must never break, and run through it before every release. Even a Google Sheet works.

Got paying customers and releasing every week or two? Start automating the flows that never change: login, signup, payments. Keep a human on everything new.

Growing fast with multiple teams? Now automation needs to run on every code push, inside your CI/CD pipeline. Your testers stop repeating old checks and spend their time actually hunting for bugs, which is the work they’re best at anyway.

One rule we like: if someone on your team has tested the same thing by hand three releases in a row, it’s time to automate it.

Is there a middle ground?

For a long time, startups were stuck. Manual was too slow. Proper automation was too expensive and too fragile for a small team.

That’s slowly changing. With scriptless test automation, testers can create tests without writing code. A good self-healing automation tool repairs tests on its own when a button moves or a label changes, so you’re not fixing red tests every morning. And AI regression testing software can pick which tests actually matter for a given change, so you’re not running everything every time.

Is it perfect? No. You still need someone who understands your product and your users. But it does mean a three-person startup can start automating much earlier than before, without hiring a dedicated automation engineer. It’s also why more companies now think of quality engineering as something that runs alongside development, not a final gate before launch.

Our take

Manual vs automation isn’t really a fight. You need human eyes for judgment and machines for repetition. The trick is shifting the balance as you grow, instead of jumping straight to a heavy automation setup on day one.

If you do one thing after reading this, make it this: write down the five user flows that would hurt most if they broke. Test those by hand for now. The moment you get tired of repeating them, that’s your signal to automate.

And if your team doesn’t have automation engineers, it’s worth looking at testing without writing a single line of code. It’s come a long way in the last couple of years.

One last thought. Testing is usually just one piece of a bigger shift. A lot of the founders we talk to are also figuring out where AI fits into their product and operations. If that’s you, it helps to work with an AI transformation partner instead of stitching together five different vendors. Someone who can handle the digital transformation consulting side, and later act as your AI governance company once AI is live, so audits and compliance don’t turn into a surprise.

Still unsure what fits your stage? Drop us a message. Happy to talk it through, no sales pitch.

medium.titulo: The Architecture POC: An Experiment, Not a Prototype
medium.resumo: How architects turn technical uncertainty into evidence for a decision.
medium.conteudo_html:
How architects turn technical uncertainty into evidence for a decision.

“It worked” may be the most dangerous conclusion a team can reach at the end of a proof of concept (POC).

Worked under what conditions? Against what baseline? And, most importantly, what architecture decision does the result allow the team to make?

A proof of concept is often treated as a miniature implementation, a vendor demonstration, or a chance to make a preferred solution look convincing. That is how teams end up with attractive demos and weak decisions.

A good POC is something narrower and more useful: a controlled experiment designed to reduce a specific uncertainty that is blocking an architecture decision.

It does not make the decision. It produces evidence for the person accountable for making it.

Use a POC only when evidence can change the decision

Not every unknown deserves a POC.

Use one when the decision has a technical uncertainty that cannot be resolved well enough through documentation, vendor material, established benchmarks, or a design review. The cost of being wrong should be meaningful: a difficult migration, a data-layer commitment, an integration contract, or a component that will be expensive to replace once it is in production.

Do not use one when the question is really organizational, political, or procedural. A load test will not tell you whether a team can own a new platform safely. A reversible choice is another poor candidate: reserve POCs for commitments that will be expensive to undo. Overusing POCs is a failure mode of its own; it delays commitment while creating the appearance of diligence.

The test is simple: if the result would not change what the team does next, do not run the POC.

Principle: A POC is justified by the value of the decision it enables, not by the novelty of the technology being explored.

A POC is not a prototype

Several useful activities are often called a POC. They are not interchangeable:

  • POC — reduces a specific, decision-blocking technical uncertainty.
  • Prototype — explores or demonstrates a possible solution.
  • Demo — shows or persuades others that a solution appears to work.
  • Spike — explores an unknown before the team has formal decision criteria; a POC begins once the question and decision rule are defined.
  • MVP — delivers the smallest version of real user value.

Each has value. Calling a prototype or demo a POC, however, does not turn its output into decision-quality evidence.

Start with the decision, then name the uncertainty

Teams often start with a technology question: “Can we use a managed queue?” or “Will this database scale?” Those questions are too broad to guide a useful experiment.

Start one step earlier:

  1. What decision must be made?
  2. What uncertainty is preventing that decision?
  3. What evidence would reduce that uncertainty enough to act?

Consider Meridian, a hypothetical SaaS analytics platform that needs to separate peak event ingestion from dashboard query serving. Its peak rate is 8,000 events per second, and its dashboard-query target is 300 ms p95. The architecture team is evaluating one candidate design: a database-backed outbox, which records an event with the business change, feeding a managed queue and a separate read model, a data store optimized for queries. The architecture decision must account for performance, auditability, and a small team’s operational constraints before a SOC 2 audit deadline.

That decision contains several questions. The POC should concentrate on the primary technical uncertainty rather than trying to settle them all at once. For example:

Can the candidate ingestion path sustain Meridian’s 8,000-event-per-second peak while keeping dashboard queries within their 300 ms p95 target and, after a consumer backlog, reconstructing an auditable record of every event’s processing outcome?

This is one question with four supporting measurements: throughput, latency, recovery behavior, and event integrity. It is specific and observable, and its result can rule the approach out. It also makes clear what the POC cannot establish: it does not, by itself, prove that the team is ready to operate the system or that every SOC 2 requirement has been satisfied.

Starting with a preferred technology and then inventing a test that makes it look successful is a common mistake. The decision has to determine the experiment, not the other way around.

Define the decision rule before writing code

The most important POC work happens before implementation begins.

Write down the success condition, the failure condition, and the ambiguous condition. Be precise about the measurement method, the load profile, and the data used. When performance matters, include a baseline: the current system, a competing candidate, a documented requirement, or all three.

The person accountable for the decision should agree to these rules before the POC begins. Otherwise, the team can still rationalize an attractive result after the fact.

For Meridian, the decision rule might look like this:

  • Owner: Meridian’s architecture lead, who is accountable for the recommendation.
  • Decision: Is the outbox, managed queue, and read-model candidate technically viable enough to proceed to architecture approval?
  • Test setup: Run five 45-minute tests at 8,000 events per second, using a production-like mix of event sizes and tenant activity. Ten minutes into each run, pause the consumer for 15 minutes while ingestion continues, then restore it and allow 20 minutes for recovery.
  • Baseline context: The current design has a dashboard-query p95 of 850 ms under the same profile. This shows the scale of the current problem; the 300 ms requirement — not percentage improvement over the baseline — is the decision threshold.
  • Success: In all five runs, dashboard-query p95 stays at or below 300 ms; the backlog clears within the 20-minute recovery window; every input event can be reconciled to one recorded processing outcome; and repeated delivery causes no duplicate business effect because the consumer is idempotent.
  • Failure: The latency target is missed in three or more runs; the backlog does not clear in the recovery window; any event cannot be reconciled after recovery; a duplicate produces a duplicate business effect; or event identity and processing lineage cannot be reconstructed for the audit record.
  • Ambiguous: The target is missed in one or two runs, results vary without an understood cause, or success depends on an assumption that cannot yet be shown to match production.

An ambiguous result is not partial success. It means the accountable decision-maker cannot yet use the POC to proceed. The next action may be to narrow the question, run a prerequisite experiment, improve the test conditions, or make the decision while explicitly accepting the remaining risk.

The specific numbers are illustrative. The discipline is to decide what they mean before seeing them; otherwise, the team can rationalize a preferred outcome after the fact.

One POC can have several related measurements, but it should have one primary question and one decision it informs. Latency, throughput, recovery time, and data integrity can all belong to the same experiment when they are necessary to answer that question. Unrelated questions should be separated or sequenced.

Scope the experiment, not a small product

The fastest way to weaken a POC is to turn it into a production-shaped project.

Define the scope partly through an explicit “will not build” list. For a narrow performance experiment, that might exclude a user interface, production-grade logging, broad edge-case support, and integrations unrelated to the test. Use mocks aggressively for components that are not the variable under examination. A representative load generator is often more valuable than a realistic frontend.

Those exclusions are defaults, not absolutes. Do not omit security, observability, error handling, or failure recovery when one of them is the question being tested. The better rule is:

Do not productionize anything unless it is required to answer the question.

Treat POC code as disposable. If the team later wants to keep it, that should be a separate decision with an explicit hardening scope. Code built only to isolate a variable carries none of the production guarantees that its appearance may imply.

Time-box the work before it starts. A focused architecture POC often takes days or a couple of weeks, but the exact duration is less important than the boundary. If the experiment keeps expanding, the team may have framed the question too broadly, uncovered a prerequisite unknown, or drifted into implementation planning. Pause and examine the framing; do not keep adding features.

Make “realistic” explicit

Many POCs pass because the test conditions quietly make success easy.

Before the first run, state what “realistic” means:

  • Volume: What data size, event rate, or request rate reflects the decision being made?
  • Concurrency: How many simultaneous users, consumers, or writers matter?
  • Data shape: Which skew, large records, malformed inputs, or missing metadata could affect the outcome?
  • Failure conditions: Which retries, slow dependencies, consumer interruptions, or backlog scenarios must be included?
  • Environment: Which versions, instance sizes, configuration values, and network assumptions define the result?

Representative data from the real system is best when it can be used safely. When it cannot, document the substitute dataset and the assumptions it makes. A result obtained with synthetic data is not invalid; it is bounded by what that data fails to represent.

Run it honestly — and make it repeatable

Version or script the load harness, environment setup, and configuration so another engineer can rerun the same experiment. Preserve the raw evidence. Run it enough times to understand variability; for Meridian, that means reporting the median and range across its five runs. Quietly changing conditions after seeing an unwanted result invalidates the comparison. If the next run tests a different threshold or configuration, say that the question has changed.

Bias is especially likely when a vendor supports the POC or its author has already championed the candidate. Vendor assistance is not inherently a problem, but it should be disclosed. Agree the decision rule and test design before any runs, then ask someone who is not invested in the preferred outcome to review the evidence and conclusion. Test a credible alternative with the same harness only when that comparison is necessary for the decision; otherwise, do not double the scope by default.

A single-candidate POC can establish viability. It cannot establish that the candidate is the best available option. That judgment still needs the wider comparison of constraints, alternatives, and consequences.

A result includes the conditions under which it worked and the limits of what that evidence supports.

Where AI helps with a POC

AI is especially useful once the POC’s decision rule is already defined. The work is bounded: the question is narrow, the inputs and failure modes are named, and the expected evidence is measurable.

It can accelerate disposable scaffolding: load generators, mocks, synthetic datasets, infrastructure setup, failure-injection scripts, test harnesses, metric queries, and ADR first drafts.

But AI should not define the proof after the fact. The success criteria, realistic conditions, and interpretation of the results still need to come from the architecture decision and be agreed before the experiment runs.

Use AI to accelerate the experiment, not to decide what the experiment proved.

End with a decision record, not a demo

A POC is complete when its evidence has been interpreted and recorded — not when someone has seen it running.

Capture the result in an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) or another decision record that includes:

  • the decision and question being addressed;
  • the approach and test conditions;
  • the measurements and their baseline or threshold;
  • the conclusion the evidence supports;
  • the assumptions and remaining unknowns; and
  • the next action: proceed, reject, investigate further, or change course.

This record is more valuable than the POC code in the long term. It explains why the team accepted or rejected an option, prevents the same question from being relitigated without new evidence, and preserves the validity limits that can otherwise disappear from memory.

Suppose Meridian records p95 dashboard latency below 280 ms in four runs, but observes 410 ms during backlog recovery in the fifth. Under the agreed rule, that is ambiguous — not a pass. Its ADR would record the recovery condition, preserve the measurements, and trigger a smaller follow-up POC into the contention causing the spike. The result has prevented a premature commitment even though it did not yet justify approval.

The conclusion should be deliberately modest. A POC may establish that an approach appears technically viable under stated conditions. It should not be presented as evidence that the full system is ready for production unless that was genuinely the experiment’s scope. For Meridian, the ADR can support the traceability evidence needed for SOC 2 review; it is not proof of SOC 2 compliance.

Rejected and inconclusive outcomes deserve the same clarity as successful ones. Present the tested conditions, what the evidence rules out, what remains unknown, and the next action. That is evidence of disciplined decision-making, not a failed exercise.

A POC brief in six lines

Before starting, write down:

  1. Decision: What must be decided, and who is accountable for it?
  2. Question: What specific technical uncertainty is blocking that decision?
  3. Decision rule: What are the baseline, success, failure, and ambiguous outcomes?
  4. Scope: What will be built, and what explicitly will not?
  5. Conditions: What load, data shape, failures, environment, and measurement method make the test meaningful?
  6. Exit: When will the POC stop, and what action follows each possible result?

Related reading

These articles use AI as a support tool, but the underlying practices apply whether or not AI is involved:

  • Clarify, Design, Critique: A Repeatable AI Workflow for Architects
  • Drafting Better ADRs with AI
  • Adversarial Design Critique: How to Get AI to Challenge Your Architecture

Know when to stop

Sometimes the most useful POC outcome is that the original question was wrong.

If every run exposes an unrelated unknown, or the results remain ambiguous after the planned work, stop and inspect the framing. The team may need a smaller prior experiment, a different decision rule, or a decision that acknowledges the uncertainty rather than pretending it has been removed.

Continuing only because time has already been spent is not rigor. It is sunk-cost thinking with test data attached.

The goal is not to eliminate all risk. Architecture cannot promise that. The goal is to replace the uncertainty that matters most with enough credible evidence to make the next decision responsibly.

A POC is not a miniature product and it is not a demo. It is a controlled experiment that turns a technical uncertainty into evidence for an architectural decision.

medium.titulo: The AI Said “Done.” Reality Said Otherwise.
medium.resumo: How a mechanical diagnostician’s question became UAEP — and why a successful tool call is not proof that the job happened.
medium.conteudo_html:
How a mechanical diagnostician’s question became UAEP — and why a successful tool call is not proof that the job happened.

The most dangerous word in an autonomous system may be the simplest one: done.

I did not arrive at that thought by trying to make a chatbot sound smarter. I was building an advanced Director Bridge and AI Production Suite so AI could do sustained work inside complex professional software. I wanted it to operate tools, carry a task forward and produce an actual result outside the conversation.

That is when “done” stopped being a sentence and became a claim about reality.

An agent could choose a plausible tool, receive a success response and report the task as 100% complete. But when I looked at the destination, the result could be wrong. The system had drifted. The wrong target had changed. Part of the work was missing. Sometimes the intended command had not reached the place that mattered.

I knew that shape of problem from another world.

Most of my working life has been spent around mechanical, electrical and computer-controlled machinery. A controller can issue a command. A relay can energise. A diagnostic display can look reassuring. None of those observations, by itself, proves that the component moved, the pressure changed or the machine reached the required state.

In a workshop, you go to the machine and check.

Why should software acting in the world get a softer standard?

The mirror broke

At first I thought I had found one problem: false completion. Fix the moment an agent says “done” too early.

But the closer I looked, the more the problem broke apart. Evidence could describe an old state. Authority could be valid when work began and gone by the time an effect occurred. Recovery could restart a process without restoring the original objective. Several individually plausible actions could combine into an outcome nobody authorised.

I began to picture a mirror hitting concrete. I had followed one crack and found a floor covered in pieces.

The question became bigger than AI: how many parts of a system can be individually “successful” while the system as a whole is still wrong?

That question led me to UAEP — Universal Agent Execution Platform. It is an execution-assurance system concerned with the gap between a reported action and a verified external outcome. AI agents are an important application, but the question also appears in ordinary software, cloud services, enterprise workflows, networks and sufficiently observable physical systems.

UAEP does not make an API response mean more than it does. It asks whether the authorised result exists at the destination, whether the evidence really applies to this case and whether a failed or recovered path actually reached the original objective. If the answer cannot be established, “unknown” is more honest than “verified.”

A workshop habit became a design rule

Some of my phrases sound more at home beside a machine than in an AI paper. The command is not the outcome. Activity is not progress. Intelligence provides the strength; assurance provides the load path.

They became useful because they forced me to look at the whole journey rather than the green light on one component.

The same thinking shaped my approach to testing. If a design failed under a certain load, I would not repair it and then celebrate because it survived an easier load. I would put the same load back on it.

So I publicly invited people to make UAEP lie: bring a reproducible case where “VERIFIED” would not be justified.

The challenges found real boundaries. One exposed a weakness in the original external assurance boundary. A later, broader execution-graph campaign exposed an enforcement failure: an effect that had been permitted could become a materially different actual effect. Detecting that after it happened was not enough.

I kept those failures in the record. I corrected the affected external boundaries, without rewriting UAEP’s core assurance relationships, and reran the preserved hostile cases.

In the final bounded, self-run synthetic successor campaign, all 29 cases were scored. It recorded zero protocol errors, zero false VERIFIED conclusions and zero false-authorised consequential effects within the tested path. Seventeen legitimate authorised effects still committed. Those numbers are not independent certification or a promise about every production environment. They are the measured result of that declared campaign — including the failures that came before it.

To me, that is a more useful story than “it was perfect from the start.”

Even the inbox proved the point

When I tried to show UAEP to major companies, I discovered an almost comic version of the original problem. An email system could acknowledge my message. An intake process could mark it forwarded. Yet I had no evidence that my real objective — getting the work in front of someone qualified to assess it — had happened.

Process success is not destination success.

I cannot force a company to look. I can make the public story available, invite serious challenge and keep the implementation confidential while I explore commercial options.

I am Adam Mangan, an independent Australian inventor. I filed an Australian provisional patent application on 16 September 2026 — application no. 2026907889. UAEP’s implementation remains confidential; the public claims are deliberately narrower than the full architecture.

The machine told me: done.

My background taught me to answer: show me.

That answer became UAEP. It is also only the first part of a wider body of work I am not yet ready to disclose.

Read the full illustrated UAEP story and explore the public site.

medium.titulo: Claude Haiku 5.5 Could Change the Default Model in Your AI Stack
medium.resumo: The AI industry usually celebrates a new model by asking one question:
medium.conteudo_html:
The AI industry usually celebrates a new model by asking one question:

How smart is it?

Claude Haiku 5.5 makes another question more interesting:

How cheaply can we run intelligence everywhere?

Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7 as its fastest and most affordable small model yet. It is designed for high-volume workloads such as classification, extraction, routing, summarization, browser use, and subagent tasks. Anthropic says it costs around 75% less to run on average than Haiku 4.5.

The headline pricing is even more aggressive.

For requests up to 100,000 input tokens, Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens.

That is 90% lower than Haiku 4.5’s list price for the same input range.

But the interesting part for software engineers is not the price itself.

It is what this price makes possible.

The expensive-model architecture is becoming harder to justify

A common AI application architecture looks like this:

User → application → large language model → response

For a simple chatbot, that can work.

Production applications are different.

A single user request may require:

  • intent classification
  • authentication checks
  • document retrieval
  • data extraction
  • summarization
  • tool selection
  • API calls
  • validation
  • formatting
  • final reasoning

If every one of those operations uses a frontier model, costs can grow quickly.

Imagine an application where a large model handles all ten internal operations.

That may produce excellent results.

But it is often economically inefficient.

You do not need a frontier reasoning model to determine whether a support ticket is about billing.

You do not need an expensive model to extract an invoice number.

You do not need the most capable model to summarize a 2,000-word document.

You probably do not need it to decide which internal API should be called.

This is where Haiku 5.5 becomes interesting.

The real product is model routing

The future architecture may look less like:

Application → best model

and more like:

Application → router → appropriate model

For example:

┌── Haiku 5.5 → classification
                    │
User request → Router ├── Haiku 5.5 → extraction
                    │
                    ├── Sonnet 5.5 → complex coding
                    │
                    └── Opus 5.5 → difficult reasoning

The model is no longer a single dependency.

It becomes one component in an inference strategy.

Haiku 5.5 is particularly suited to this architecture because Anthropic explicitly positions it for high-volume tasks and as a subagent alongside larger Claude models.

This changes how developers should think about model selection.

The question is no longer:

“Which model should power my application?”

It becomes:

“Which model should handle each class of work?”

That is a much more interesting engineering problem.

Haiku 5.5 is not trying to replace Opus

Anthropic is very clear about the positioning.

Haiku 5.5 is not the best choice for every complex coding problem.

On Anthropic’s published Terminal-Bench 4.0 results, Haiku 5.5 scored 39.2%, compared with 70.6% for Sonnet 5.5. On FrontierCode 1.1 Main, Haiku 5.5 reached 46.4%, while Sonnet 5.5 reached 52.1% at the reported xhigh setting.

That distinction matters.

The point is not:

Haiku 5.5 beats every larger model.

The point is:

Haiku 5.5 is capable enough that many small tasks no longer need a larger model.

That is potentially more important for application architecture.

Consider an AI coding agent.

A large model might be responsible for:

  • understanding the task
  • planning the implementation
  • making architectural decisions
  • reviewing the final result

But dozens of smaller operations happen around that central task.

An agent may need to:

  • inspect a file
  • summarize a module
  • classify an error
  • extract a function signature
  • identify relevant files
  • compress context
  • check a command result
  • decide whether a tool call is necessary

Those are exactly the kinds of workloads where a cheaper model can become valuable.

This is where AI agents get interesting

Agentic software has a hidden cost problem.

One user request can produce many model calls.

For example:

User request
     ↓
Planner
     ↓
Repository search
     ↓
File classification
     ↓
Context extraction
     ↓
Code generation
     ↓
Test analysis
     ↓
Error classification
     ↓
Correction
     ↓
Final review

If every arrow represents a call to a premium model, the cost of one task can become surprisingly high.

Now imagine an engineering platform serving thousands of developers.

The number of model calls becomes enormous.

Haiku 5.5 gives developers another option:

Complex reasoning → Sonnet / Opus
Routine agent work → Haiku
High-volume classification → Haiku
Extraction → Haiku
Routing → Haiku
Summarization → Haiku

The expensive model becomes the specialist.

The cheaper model becomes the workforce surrounding it.

That is a fundamentally different architecture.

The 1M-token context window makes the small-model label misleading

There is another detail developers should not overlook.

Haiku 5.5 has a 1 million token context window and supports up to 128,000 output tokens.

Calling it a “small model” therefore describes its position in Anthropic’s model family more than the size of the workloads it can see.

This matters for software engineering.

Consider a large repository.

An agent may need to reason about:

  • architecture documentation
  • API contracts
  • database schemas
  • configuration
  • source files
  • tests
  • previous tool results
  • issue descriptions

A model with a large context window can potentially process much more of that information without aggressive context reduction.

But there is an important catch.

Large context does not automatically mean cheap context.

Haiku 5.5’s pricing changes significantly above 100,000 input tokens.

For prompts up to 100K tokens, the listed input/output prices are $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens.

Above 100K, they become $0.50/$2.50.

So developers still need to design context carefully.

A 1M-token context window is a capability.

It is not an instruction to send 1M tokens on every request.

There is another engineering change: adaptive thinking

Haiku 5.5 is also the first Haiku-class model with an adjustable effort setting.

Adaptive thinking is enabled by default, allowing the model to determine when and how much reasoning to perform. Developers can control the tradeoff using the effort parameter.

This introduces an important concept:

Inference quality can become a runtime setting.

Instead of choosing only between:

cheap model
vs.
expensive model

you can increasingly choose:

same model
+
different reasoning effort

That opens another optimization layer.

For example:

Simple classification
→ low effort
Normal extraction
→ medium effort
Ambiguous task
→ higher effort
Complex reasoning
→ escalate to larger model

This is much closer to how traditional software systems are optimized.

You do not give every request maximum CPU.

You allocate resources according to workload.

AI applications are moving in the same direction.

The biggest opportunity may be AI infrastructure, not chatbots

This is why Haiku 5.5 is particularly interesting to developers.

The strongest use cases may not be visible to end users.

A user might see:

“Your report is ready.”

Behind the scenes, the system could have used five different AI calls.

One model determines the document type.

Another extracts information.

Another checks for missing fields.

Another summarizes the results.

A larger model performs the final reasoning.

The user does not care which model performed each operation.

They care about:

  • correctness
  • latency
  • reliability
  • price

That means model routing can become an infrastructure layer, similar to databases, queues, caches, and API gateways.

Haiku 5.5 is already moving into developer tools

This is not limited to API experiments.

GitHub has already made Claude Haiku 5.5 generally available in GitHub Copilot for supported plans and developer environments, including VS Code, Visual Studio, Copilot CLI, cloud agent, JetBrains IDEs, Xcode, Eclipse, and other Copilot surfaces. GitHub positions it for fast, high-volume work such as subagents, quick edits, and terminal tasks.

GitHub’s early testing also found Haiku 5.5 matched Claude Sonnet 5 on many coding tasks while using fewer tokens and steps.

That is exactly the kind of workload where model economics matter.

An AI coding agent may perform dozens of relatively small operations before producing one meaningful pull request.

The best model for the final code change may not be the best model for everything around it.

Developers should stop measuring only tokens per request

There is an important trap here.

Cheap tokens do not automatically mean cheap applications.

The actual metric should be:

cost per successful task

Suppose Model A costs $1 per million tokens but requires ten attempts.

Model B costs $3 per million tokens but solves the task in two attempts.

Model B could be cheaper overall.

Haiku 5.5’s economics become interesting precisely because Anthropic reports improvements in both capability and efficiency.

For example, Anthropic cites customer testing from Asana, HubSpot, AlphaSense, Box, Rogo, and Cognition showing improvements in latency, accuracy, or cost for specific workloads. One AlphaSense workload, for example, involved roughly 8 million calls per week.

At that scale, even small efficiency improvements become meaningful.

A few cents saved per thousand requests becomes thousands of dollars when multiplied across millions of operations.

There is also a migration trap

If you are currently using Haiku 4.5, upgrading is not simply:

claude-haiku-4-5
        ↓
claude-haiku-5-5

Anthropic’s migration documentation highlights several behavioral changes.

Haiku 5.5 uses a newer tokenizer, meaning the same text produces approximately 30% more tokens than on Haiku 4.5, although the exact increase depends on the content. Developers therefore need to revisit token budgets and cost estimates.

There are also changes around thinking blocks.

Responses can begin with thinking blocks, so code that assumes the first content block is always the final answer needs to select blocks by their type instead.

This is a useful reminder:

Model upgrades are software migrations.

Treat them like dependency upgrades.

Run regression tests.

Measure latency.

Measure actual token usage.

Check structured outputs.

Verify tool calling.

Test edge cases.

Then compare cost per successful task.

Do not simply change the model ID and deploy.

The future may have no “default model”

This may be the most important lesson from Haiku 5.5.

For years, developers asked:

Which model should I use?

The next generation of AI applications may ask:

Which model should I use for this operation?

That sounds like a small difference.

Architecturally, it is enormous.

A mature AI application may eventually have:

Router model

determines what needs to happen.

Fast model

handles high-volume routine work.

Reasoning model

handles difficult decisions.

Coding model

handles implementation.

Vision model

handles visual inputs.

Embedding model

handles retrieval.

Validator

checks the result.

Human

handles the cases the system cannot confidently resolve.

The application becomes an orchestration system rather than a wrapper around one LLM.

Claude Haiku 5.5 fits particularly well into that future because it is cheap enough, fast enough, and capable enough to occupy many of the lower-cost layers.

The real Haiku 5.5 story is not “small model gets smarter”

That headline is easy to write.

The more important story is:

AI intelligence is becoming cheaper to distribute.

When intelligence becomes cheap enough, developers start putting it in places where they previously could not justify it.

Inside routers.

Inside background jobs.

Inside browser automation.

Inside coding agents.

Inside document pipelines.

Inside customer-support workflows.

Inside data processing systems.

Inside validation layers.

Inside internal developer tools.

That is when AI stops being a single feature and starts becoming infrastructure.

Claude Haiku 5.5 is not the model you necessarily choose for the hardest problem.

It may be the model you choose for the hundreds of smaller problems surrounding the hardest one.

And that could be much more important for software engineering.

The future of AI applications may not belong to the system using the smartest model everywhere.

It may belong to the system that knows where expensive intelligence is actually necessary.

medium.titulo: What Is an MCP Server? I Built One in 20 Minutes (Copy My Code)
medium.resumo: What an MCP server actually is, how MCP differs from a normal API, and a working Python MCP server you can connect to Claude today. Tested…
medium.conteudo_html:
What an MCP server actually is, how MCP differs from a normal API, and a working Python MCP server you can connect to Claude today. Tested on the new MCP SDK 2.x.

TL;DR: An MCP server is a small program that gives an AI app (like Claude) new abilities: tools it can call, data it can read, and prompts it can use, all through one open standard called the Model Context Protocol. You write a server once, and any MCP-compatible app can use it. Below I explain how it works, how MCP compares to an API, and build a real MCP server in about 40 lines of Python, then connect it to Claude Code.

What is an MCP server?

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It’s an open standard, created by Anthropic, for connecting AI applications to outside tools and data.

An MCP server is the program on the other end of that connection. It tells the AI: “Here’s what I can do, and here’s how to ask me.”

The easiest way to think about it is USB-C for AI. Before USB-C, every device needed its own cable. Before MCP, every AI app needed custom code for every tool. Now:

  • A tool builder writes one MCP server.
  • Every MCP-compatible app (Claude, AI coding tools, agents) can use it right away.

Without MCP: every app × every tool. With MCP: build once, plug in anywhere.

How does MCP work?

There are three parts:

  1. Host: the AI app you use, like Claude Code or Claude Desktop.
  2. Client: the connector inside the host. It keeps one connection per server.
  3. Server: your program, which exposes abilities and talks to the real world (files, APIs, databases).

When the host starts, it asks each server “what can you do?”. The server replies with a list of its abilities, and the AI decides when to use them. The two sides talk in JSON, either over standard input/output (for local servers) or over HTTP (for remote ones).

The AI never touches your database directly. The MCP server does, on its behalf.

What can an MCP server expose?

An MCP server can offer three kinds of things:

  • Tools: actions the AI can run, like “check this website”, “query this database” or “create a GitHub issue”. This is what most servers are about.
  • Resources: data the AI can read for context, like files, documents or database rows.
  • Prompts: reusable prompt templates the user can pick, like “review this PR”.

MCP vs API: what’s the difference?

This is the most-searched MCP question right now, and the answer is simple: MCP doesn’t replace APIs. It wraps them for AI.

  • Built for: Regular API: Developers writing code; MCP server: AI models deciding what to call
  • Discovery: Regular API: You read the docs; MCP server: AI asks “what can you do?” at runtime
  • Integration: Regular API: Custom code per app; MCP server: One server works in every MCP app
  • Format: Regular API: Different for every API; MCP server: One standard protocol

An API is for developers. An MCP server makes that API usable by AI.

Most MCP servers are thin layers on top of an existing API. The GitHub MCP server calls the GitHub API, for example. The MCP layer just describes it in a way an AI can discover and use.

MCP vs RAG? They solve different problems. RAG finds relevant text and pastes it into the prompt. MCP lets the AI take actions and fetch live data on demand. RAG isn’t obsolete: many MCP servers use RAG-style search behind a tool.

Build an MCP server in 20 minutes (Python)

Let’s build something useful: a site-checker MCP server. It lets Claude check whether any website is up, how fast it responds, and what its page title is. It uses only Python’s standard library plus the MCP SDK, and it needs no API keys.

Heads up: the MCP Python SDK is now version 2.x. FastMCP was renamed to MCPServer, so many older tutorials no longer run. The code below is tested on SDK 2.3.0.

Four steps from empty folder to Claude using your tool.

Step 1: Set up the project

You need Python 3.10 or newer.

mkdir site-checker && cd site-checker
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install "mcp[cli]"

Step 2: Write the server

Create server.py:

import time
import urllib.request
from html.parser import HTMLParser
from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer
mcp = MCPServer("site-checker")
class TitleParser(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.in_title, self.title = False, ""
    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        self.in_title = tag == "title"
    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        self.in_title = False
    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.in_title:
            self.title += data
@mcp.tool()
def check_website(url: str) -> dict:
    """Check if a website is up. Returns status code, response time and page title."""
    if not url.startswith("http"):
        url = "https://" + url
    start = time.time()
    try:
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "site-checker"})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) as res:
            parser = TitleParser()
            parser.feed(res.read(200_000).decode("utf-8", "ignore"))
            return {"url": url, "up": True, "status": res.status,
                    "ms": round((time.time() - start) * 1000), "title": parser.title.strip()}
    except Exception as e:
        return {"url": url, "up": False, "error": str(e)}
if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

Three things make this an MCP server:

  • MCPServer("site-checker") creates the server.
  • @mcp.tool() turns a normal Python function into a tool. The docstring becomes the description the AI reads, so write it clearly.
  • mcp.run() starts the server over standard input/output.

The type hints (url: str, -> dict) matter too. The SDK turns them into a schema, so the AI knows exactly what to send.

Step 3: Connect it to Claude Code

claude mcp add site-checker -- /full/path/to/site-checker/.venv/bin/python /full/path/to/site-checker/server.py

Use full paths. Then start Claude Code and run /mcp to check that site-checker shows up as connected.

Step 4: Use it

Just ask in plain English:

Is example.com up? How fast does it respond?

Claude sees the check_website tool, calls it, and answers with real data:

{"url": "https://example.com", "up": true, "status": 200, "ms": 357, "title": "Example Domain"}

If a site is down, the tool returns "up": false with the error, so Claude can tell you why it failed instead of guessing.

That’s it. You built an MCP server. Every new ability is now one more decorated function.

MCP servers worth installing

Once you get the idea, you’ll want more. These are the kinds of MCP servers I use every day:

  • Browser automation (Playwright): Claude opens real pages, clicks around and takes screenshots to check its own UI work.
  • Your database (Supabase, Postgres): query data and run migrations from the chat.
  • GitHub: issues, PRs and code search.
  • SEO data: live keyword volumes and Google results. This article’s keywords came from one.
  • Docs servers: up-to-date library docs, so the AI stops using old APIs.

MCP security: read this before installing servers

An MCP server runs code with your permissions. Treat installing one like installing any app:

  • Only install servers from sources you trust, and read the code if you can.
  • Keep API keys in environment variables (claude mcp add ... -e API_KEY=...), never in your prompts.
  • Give a server the smallest access it needs, like read-only database credentials when reading is enough.
  • Be careful with servers that read untrusted content (web pages, emails). That text can contain instructions aimed at the AI.

FAQ

What does MCP stand for?

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools, data and prompts.

What is an MCP server in simple terms?

A small program that gives an AI new abilities, like checking a website, reading a database or creating a GitHub issue, in a standard format any MCP-compatible AI app can use.

How is MCP different from an API?

An API is designed for developers who read docs and write integration code. An MCP server describes its abilities so an AI can discover and use them at runtime. Most MCP servers are built on top of existing APIs.

What is MCP vs RAG?

RAG retrieves relevant text and adds it to the prompt. MCP lets the AI call tools and fetch live data on demand. They work well together.

Is RAG obsolete with MCP?

No. RAG is still the best way to search large document collections. MCP is a way to expose that search (and other actions) to an AI as a tool.

Does ChatGPT use MCP?

MCP is an open standard and is no longer Claude-only. OpenAI, GitHub Copilot and many AI coding tools have added MCP support, so one server can work across several apps.

Do I need to know Python to build an MCP server?

No. There are official SDKs for several languages, including TypeScript. Python is just one of the shortest ways to start.

More in this series: How to Use Claude Code: The Exact Workflow I Use to Ship Sites Solo and Claude Skills Explained: How to Build Your Own (+ the 10 I Actually Use). I’m an AI engineer and solo founder writing practical guides on Claude, AI agents and LLMs. Follow me for the next one.

medium.titulo: Quasar Framework em 2026: ainda vale a pena?
medium.resumo: Uma visão rápida sobre o estado atual do Quasar, Vite 8, MCP, IA e por que o framework continua sendo uma opção forte para aplicações…
medium.conteudo_html:
Uma visão rápida sobre o estado atual do Quasar, Vite 8, MCP, IA e por que o framework continua sendo uma opção forte para aplicações multiplataforma.

Existe uma pergunta que aparece com frequência no ecossistema frontend:

“Quasar ainda faz sentido em 2026?”

Com tantos frameworks surgindo, novas ferramentas de build, aplicações cada vez mais orientadas a IA e a popularização de stacks como Next.js, Nuxt e outras soluções modernas, é natural questionar se um framework criado há alguns anos ainda é uma boa escolha para novos projetos.

Minha resposta curta é:

Sim. E 2026 talvez seja um dos anos mais interessantes para o Quasar.

Mas não necessariamente pelas razões que fizeram o framework ficar conhecido originalmente.

O Quasar está passando por uma modernização importante, aproximando sua infraestrutura das ferramentas mais atuais do ecossistema JavaScript, enquanto mantém seu principal diferencial:

um único projeto Vue capaz de atender diferentes plataformas.

Conheça o Vue.js Expert

O diferencial continua sendo multiplataforma

O Quasar nunca foi apenas uma biblioteca de componentes para Vue.

Essa é talvez uma das maiores confusões sobre o framework.

A proposta é muito mais próxima de uma plataforma de desenvolvimento.

A partir de uma mesma base de código, é possível trabalhar com:

  • SPA
  • SSR
  • SSG
  • PWA
  • aplicações mobile
  • aplicações Electron
  • extensões de navegador

Tudo isso integrado ao ecossistema do Quasar CLI.

E esse modelo continua extremamente interessante para determinados tipos de produto.

Imagine, por exemplo, um sistema corporativo.

Você pode ter:

Web

Uma aplicação acessada pelo navegador.

Mobile

Uma versão utilizada por equipes externas, vendedores ou técnicos em campo.

Desktop

Uma aplicação instalada para determinados usuários internos.

PWA

Uma alternativa para situações em que instalar um aplicativo não faz sentido.

Em vez de criar quatro projetos completamente diferentes, o Quasar permite manter grande parte da lógica, componentes e estrutura compartilhados.

Isso não significa que absolutamente tudo será igual em todas as plataformas.

Mas significa que o custo de manter essas plataformas pode ser significativamente menor.

E é justamente aqui que o Quasar continua tendo uma vantagem difícil de ignorar.

2026 trouxe uma mudança importante: Vite virou o centro

Uma das mudanças mais importantes do ecossistema Quasar aconteceu justamente na infraestrutura.

O projeto decidiu abandonar progressivamente o @quasar/app-webpack e concentrar o desenvolvimento no @quasar/app-vite.

A decisão é bastante coerente com o movimento do próprio ecossistema frontend.

Em 2026, o @quasar/app-vite chegou à versão 3, enquanto o suporte ao Webpack foi oficialmente descontinuado em favor de uma estratégia centrada em Vite.

E isso trouxe uma modernização considerável.

O novo app-vite passou a utilizar Vite 8 e adotou Rolldown em sua arquitetura interna.

O próprio Vite 8 representa uma mudança importante: o projeto passou a utilizar Rolldown como bundler unificado, baseado em Rust, substituindo a antiga combinação entre esbuild e Rollup.

O Quasar acompanhou esse movimento.

Além do Vite 8, o novo app-vite também trouxe mudanças internas envolvendo:

Ele está se alinhando com a direção atual do frontend.

E o Vite 8 não é apenas uma troca de versão

Para quem acompanha o ecossistema JavaScript, Vite deixou de ser apenas uma ferramenta de desenvolvimento rápida.

Ele está se tornando uma peça central da infraestrutura moderna de frontend.

Por isso, a adoção do Vite 8 pelo Quasar é mais significativa do que simplesmente dizer:

“Agora o Quasar usa uma versão mais nova do Vite.”

Isso também facilita a vida de desenvolvedores que já trabalham com Vite em outros projetos.

Quasar não precisa competir com Vite.

Ele pode utilizar Vite como infraestrutura e concentrar seu valor naquilo que faz melhor:

componentes + CLI + arquitetura multiplataforma + integração com mobile/desktop + ferramentas de desenvolvimento.

SSG também entrou em cena

Nuxt continua sendo uma opção extremamente forte para determinados cenários.

Mas o espaço de possibilidades do Quasar aumentou.

O ponto mais interessante de 2026: MCP

Talvez uma das novidades mais interessantes para quem desenvolve atualmente seja outra:

o Quasar ficou preparado para agentes de IA.

O projeto passou a disponibilizar o @quasar/mcp, um servidor baseado no Model Context Protocol.

A ideia é simples, mas poderosa.

Um agente de programação não precisa mais depender apenas do conhecimento que recebeu durante seu treinamento.

Ele pode consultar a documentação e a API da versão do Quasar instalada no projeto.

Isso resolve um problema bastante comum com ferramentas de IA.

Imagine que seu projeto utiliza uma versão específica do Quasar.

Você pergunta ao seu agente:

“Como configuro esse componente?”

O modelo pode conhecer uma API de outra versão.

Pode sugerir uma propriedade que não existe.

Pode utilizar uma configuração antiga.

Ou simplesmente inventar alguma coisa que parece plausível.

  • props;
  • slots;
  • eventos;
  • métodos;
  • plugins;
  • composables;
  • utilitários;
  • configurações do CLI.

Para uma fase em que:

E o Quasar já está adotando esse modelo.

Quasar + IA é uma combinação interessante para times

O MCP não está tentando transformar o Quasar em um “framework de IA”.

Ele está fazendo algo muito mais pragmático:

tornando o framework mais legível para agentes de programação.

E o Quasar UI?

Isso é especialmente valioso em aplicações grandes.

Porque, conforme o projeto cresce, ter componentes prontos deixa de ser apenas uma questão de velocidade.

Passa a ser uma questão de governança da interface.

Mas Quasar não é para todo projeto

É importante deixar isso claro.

Não acredito que exista um framework universalmente melhor.

Se estou criando um projeto extremamente focado em conteúdo e SEO, provavelmente vou avaliar Nuxt.

Se estou entrando em um ecossistema React já consolidado, provavelmente não faz sentido introduzir Vue apenas por causa do Quasar.

Se estou construindo uma pequena landing page, provavelmente não preciso de toda a estrutura oferecida pelo framework.

Mas existem cenários onde a proposta do Quasar continua extremamente convincente.

uma aplicação complexa que precisa existir em mais de uma plataforma.

Onde eu consideraria Quasar em 2026?

Sistemas corporativos

ERPs, CRMs, dashboards, sistemas administrativos e plataformas internas.

Produtos SaaS

Principalmente quando existe necessidade de uma interface rica e consistente.

Aplicações multiplataforma

Quando web, mobile e desktop fazem parte do roadmap.

Produtos para operações em campo

Aplicações utilizadas por equipes externas, vendedores, técnicos ou operações que precisam de experiência mobile.

Projetos que precisam de PWA

Quando a instalação tradicional de um aplicativo não é necessariamente necessária.

Times Vue que querem produtividade

Especialmente equipes que preferem uma solução mais integrada em vez de montar várias ferramentas independentes.

O verdadeiro diferencial talvez seja o ecossistema integrado

Quando avaliamos frameworks modernos, muitas vezes comparamos apenas:

“Qual deles tem os melhores componentes?”

Acho que essa comparação ficou pequena.

Em 2026, precisamos olhar para algo maior:

Qual stack permite que meu time entregue e mantenha o produto com menos complexidade?

Nesse sentido, o Quasar oferece uma combinação bastante interessante:

Vue + TypeScript + Vite + componentes + CLI + PWA + SSR + SSG + Mobile + Electron + MCP

Tudo isso dentro de uma mesma visão arquitetural.

E esse é um diferencial importante.

O que esperar do Quasar daqui para frente?

Isso também é interessante para quem está começando um projeto agora.

Você não precisa necessariamente esperar pelo Quasar 3.

O ecossistema atual continua ativo, enquanto a próxima grande versão está sendo construída.

E a direção parece bastante clara:

Vite-first, multiplataforma e cada vez mais preparado para desenvolvimento assistido por IA.

Então, Quasar ainda vale a pena em 2026?

Na minha opinião, sim.

Mas talvez a pergunta correta não seja:

“Quasar ainda está vivo?”

A pergunta deveria ser:

“Meu produto se beneficia de uma arquitetura multiplataforma integrada?”

Se a resposta for sim, eu definitivamente colocaria Quasar entre as tecnologias avaliadas.

Porque enquanto boa parte do frontend está discutindo qual framework usar para construir uma aplicação web, o Quasar continua fazendo uma pergunta diferente:

“E se você pudesse construir web, mobile e desktop a partir da mesma base?”

Em 2026, essa proposta continua extremamente relevante.

E agora ela vem acompanhada de uma infraestrutura muito mais moderna:

Vite 8.
Rolldown.
SSG.
TypeScript.
MCP.

Vue 3.
E uma estratégia cada vez mais focada em multiplataforma.

Mas para times que precisam construir produtos robustos, multiplataforma e sustentáveis, ele definitivamente continua sendo uma tecnologia que merece estar no radar.

Para onde o frontend está indo?

O frontend está ficando cada vez mais fragmentado em ferramentas, plataformas e agentes.

Nesse cenário, existe uma vantagem enorme em ter uma stack que consegue abstrair parte dessa complexidade.

Mas porque ele tenta resolver uma questão maior:

como uma equipe pequena ou grande pode construir e manter um produto em múltiplas plataformas sem multiplicar a complexidade do código?

Para determinados produtos, essa pergunta vale mais do que qualquer benchmark.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: O que DEU ERRADO nas inscrições da MURALHA MARATHON?
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Caos na abertura das inscrições da Muralha Marathon, com falhas na plataforma e cobranças múltiplas. Revelada a medalha da 50ª Maratona de Nova York. E mais: o calendário do Mountain Do 2027, um novo circuito de maratonas na Austrália e o patrocínio da Adidas ao Time Brasil.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quinta-feira | 8 de outubro de 2026

A abertura das inscrições para a Muralha Marathon gerou grande expectativa, mas acabou em frustração geral para muitos corredores. A organização, que nunca havia enfrentado problemas em seus processos de inscrição, decidiu trocar a plataforma Ticket Sports pela Move Now, ligada ao Foco Radical. A mudança, no entanto, resultou em um verdadeiro caos: o site apresentou instabilidade, e diversos corredores relataram cobranças múltiplas no cartão de crédito ao tentar garantir a vaga, sem receber a confirmação. Alguns chegaram a ser cobrados três vezes ou mais. A Move Now publicou um comunicado sobre a “instabilidade momentânea”, e a organização da Muralha Marathon pediu desculpas pelos transtornos, afirmando que aprenderá com os erros e trabalhará para corrigir os problemas. Quem ainda estiver com alguma pendência deve entrar em contato pelo e-mail: co*****@**********om.br.

Revelada a medalha da 50ª Maratona de Nova York

A organização da Maratona de Nova York revelou a medalha da sua 50ª edição, que acontecerá este ano. Para criar expectativa, eles publicaram no dia anterior um carrossel com todas as 49 medalhas da história da prova. A nova medalha, descrita como “linda e maravilhosa”, foi apresentada ao lado da medalha da primeira edição, destacando a evolução do design ao longo de cinco décadas.

Mountain Do anuncia calendário 2027

O circuito de trail run Mountain Do, conhecido por proporcionar experiências marcantes, já divulgou seu calendário completo para 2027. O circuito passará por 10 etapas em 5 países, oferecendo provas em locais como Colônia do Sacramento (Uruguai), Praia do Rosa (SC), Deserto da Namíbia, Chapada dos Veadeiros (GO), Costão do Santinho (SC), Fim do Mundo (Ushuaia, Argentina), Fernando de Noronha (PE), Selva Amazônica (Macapá, AP), Deserto do Saara (Marrocos) e Pantanal (MS).

Novo circuito de maratonas na Austrália

Foi anunciado um novo circuito de maratonas na Austrália, o “Atlas Major Marathons”. O desafio consiste em completar quatro provas: a Maratona de Hobart, a Maratona de Brisbane, a 7 Cairns Marathon e a Sunshine Coast Marathon. Os corredores que concluírem todas as quatro corridas receberão uma medalha especial no formato de mandala.

Revezamento da Tocha de Los Angeles 2028

O revezamento da tocha olímpica para os Jogos de Los Angeles 2028 promete ser o maior já realizado nos Estados Unidos. A tocha passará por todos os 50 estados americanos. A organização relembra que, em 1984, na mesma cidade, foi a primeira vez que pessoas comuns puderam comprar o direito de carregar a tocha, uma prática que se tornou comum desde então.

Adidas é a nova patrocinadora do COB

Você sabia que o Comitê Olímpico do Brasil (COB) agora é patrocinado pela Adidas? A parceria foi firmada em 12 de maio de 2025, e a marca passará a vestir o Time Brasil a partir de 2026, com estreia nos Jogos Olímpicos de Inverno de Milão-Cortina. O contrato cobre o ciclo olímpico até os Jogos de Los Angeles 2028, incluindo também os Jogos Pan-Americanos de 2027. A Adidas assume o lugar das marcas Peak e Riachuelo, que vestiram a delegação brasileira em Paris 2024.
